personal project

A notebook
that travels better

I've worked with leather as a hobby for over a decade. What began as an interest in craft gradually became an interest in how materials, construction, and small details shape the experience of using an object.

Over time, I found myself more interested in making things that are practical, durable, and quietly enjoyable to live with.

This notebook cover came from my own travel routine. I travel often, and the one I had was functional — but it kept bothering me in small ways.

01 / 06
The problem

While travelling, I usually carry a notebook alongside my passport and documents.

For a period I used an A6 Filofax, but the ring mechanism interrupted the writing experience and prevented the notebook from lying flat.

I returned to the Midori Traveller’s Notebook system for its flexibility and portability, though over time several aspects of the object started to feel unresolved in use.

01
The leather collects dust and fibres

The rough flesh side faces inward, so it collects dust and paper fibres with regular use. Over time, it starts to look dirty rather than naturally worn. The texture is intended to feel raw and tactile, but I found it difficult to maintain in daily travel.

02
The cover is thicker than it needs to be

At around 2mm thick, it adds weight and bulk without contributing much additional structure. For something carried daily through airports and in pockets, I wanted something lighter and easier to handle.

03
The lead seal changes quickly with use

The lead seal oxidises and deforms relatively quickly, which changes the appearance of the notebook sooner than I would want.

04
The colour palette reinforced the wrong qualities

The available colours leaned heavily toward dark browns and black. On a material that already picks up dust and visible wear easily, the overall effect felt heavier and more worn than I wanted.

02 / 06
The decisions

Each decision came from extended daily use — reducing bulk, improving durability, and making the notebook feel cleaner and more considered over time.

Leather
Crazy Horse leather, 2mm — heavy, rough-surfaced, collects wear quicklySmooth calfskin, 1.4mm. Commonly used in structured leather goods — lighter, cleaner to handle, and more refined in the way it ages.
Dyeing
Surface-dyed or undyedAniline-dyed through the entire hide. Scratches, edges, and worn areas retain the same teal rather than exposing a lighter base underneath.
Finish
Raw, untreatedBurnished throughout with Seiwa colourless gum — including the flesh side, edges, and elastic holes. Seals the fibres, reduces fraying, and gives the notebook a cleaner finish in daily use.
Hardware
Lead closure sealSolid brass. Chosen for the way it wears over time, and for the warmer contrast it creates against the teal leather.
Closure
Standard cord wrapA colour-matched elastic closure designed to visually recede into the object. Anchored through a burnished punched hole with a solid brass stud.

Interior open flat. Brass hardware at spine, elastic loops for inserts.

03 / 06
The object

Front. Brass anchor, matched elastic closure.

Brass through a burnished punch-hole. Chosen to last, not to decorate.

Loaded: passport, notebook, pen, flat pockets for tickets and receipts.

04 / 06
The inserts

The inserts are modular — held by elastic, not stitched in. The configuration changes with the trip. Nothing is fixed. Any standard refill fits. You can also make your own.

Flat pocket for tickets or receipts, held with elastic band.

The sealed pocket holds coins or small objects.

Pen sits flat. Inserts slide in without catching.

05 / 06
In use

Everything in. The cover holds its shape and opens without resistance.

The elastic closure doubles as a way to carry something personal. Mine is a gift.

I made a larger one when I need to take proper notes.

Working with leather for over a decade taught me to think carefully about how things function, feel, and age. I'm drawn to solutions that are both useful and enjoyable — where simplicity, material, and construction come together naturally.
